size.note: Shoulder height (35–50 cm), head-and-body length (69–81 cm), tail (30–41 cm) and mass follow Wikipedia, which gives 6.5–14 kg (rounded here to 7–14 kg). Animal Diversity Web gives 7–12 kg, with males 7.3–12 kg and females seldom above 10 kg. The Wikipedia range is entered; the ADW disagreement is noted.

summary: A greyish jackal with a pale stripe along each side and a white tail tip. It is more secretive and more often nocturnal than the black-backed jackal, and is the less often seen of the two jackals in Kruger.
description: The side-striped jackal is a little greyer and less contrastingly marked than the black-backed jackal. A pale, often whitish stripe runs along each side, and the bushy tail has a white tip, which is a useful field mark at night. The ears are smaller and more rounded than in the black-backed jackal. Sexes are similar in colour.
habits: It is typically monogamous and lives in pairs or small family groups. It is more omnivorous and often more nocturnal than the black-backed jackal, and is less often seen on open roads in daylight. It occurs widely in well-wooded country.

diet.summary: An opportunistic omnivore, taking fruit, insects, small vertebrates and carrion, and generally less dependent on hunting than the black-backed jackal.

young: In southern Africa, breeding is usually between June and November. Gestation is 57–70 days. Litters are of 3–6 young.
habitat: Woodland and well-vegetated savanna, including the edges of rest camps and quieter roads. It is often recorded in the central and northern parts of Kruger.

similar.note: The black-backed jackal has a sharp silver-and-black saddle, reddish flanks, and a black tail tip rather than a white one.

population.notes: No Kruger population figure was found. The EWT 2025 assessment says the majority of the regional population is in Kruger and gives a regional estimate of 1,627–9,382 mature individuals; that range is not a Kruger census and is not entered as a park figure.

viewNotes.note: A pale stripe along the side and a white tail tip distinguish it from the black-backed jackal.
The white tail tip is often the clearest mark when the animal is moving, especially at night.
